body.heading: Meet the earworm
paragraphs: An earworm is a short piece of music — often just a chorus or a jingle — that repeats in your mind without you choosing it. Researchers who study them call the experience involuntary musical imagery, and surveys suggest most people experience it regularly.

The songs that stick tend to be simple, repetitive, and familiar, with a melody that rises and falls in an easy-to-follow shape. Advertising jingles are engineered to be exactly that, which is why they are champion earworms.

body.heading: Why the loop will not stop
paragraphs: One explanation is that the brain treats an unfinished pattern as an open task. A half-remembered chorus is incomplete, so the mind keeps replaying it, the way it returns to an unsolved problem or an interrupted job.

Earworms are more likely when you are tired, stressed, or doing something automatic like walking or washing up — moments when the mind has spare capacity and a musical memory can wander in and take the stage.

body.heading: How to evict a stubborn song
paragraphs: Researchers and sufferers suggest a few tricks: listen to the whole song once, since finishing it can close the loop; switch to a different, absorbing tune; or occupy the verbal part of your mind with conversation, reading aloud, or a word puzzle.
Most earworms fade on their own within hours. Far from being a flaw, they show how powerfully music is stored — your brain kept the song safe enough to replay it without asking.

takeaway: Earworms happen when your brain loops an unfinished, catchy fragment of music — hearing the full song or giving your mind another task usually closes the loop.
